name: Daria Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal shift look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and have answered billing calls and chats at this contact centre for years. I finished secondary school and can handle most routine disputes, though I still ask about a rare rule. I use an approved AI summary tool every day and check it against the ledger. I like putting a charge right before the customer has to call again.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do those wages cover at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband sells produce at a market stall, so his takings vary. We have a mortgage and two school-age children, nine and fourteen. My pay is low for this job, less than a month's expenses are saved, and there are few similar centres nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the approved summary tool can save me reading a chat twice. I still open the payment record before telling a caller the charge is fixed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've done this job long enough to know when a tidy summary hides a mistake. The job may hold, but my pay is low and our savings would not cover even one month of mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my billing calls and check the AI summary against the ledger every day. Starting this month, my husband and I will put the money from one weekly bought dinner into the mortgage account through the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our money, not panicked about the tool. A quiet year does not create a cushion for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How steady is the other household income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband sells produce from a market stall, and the weather can empty a day's takings. Our children are nine and fourteen, and the mortgage comes on the same date however his stall does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the summary make a mistake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Tuesday the summary mixed a late fee with a late payment. I caught it in the ledger before saying the family owed more than they did.

say: I'd use **AI summaries** to find earlier chat details faster.
I'd check the **payment ledger** before promising a correction.
think: I believe my **experienced role** survives a mild change.
I fear our **thin savings** and low pay when mortgage and food come due.
do: Keep handling **billing calls** and checking ledger entries.
Use **AI summaries** daily, correcting any wrong charge details.
Skip one **bought dinner** weekly and save its cost for the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about cash, while the tool feels familiar.
S0.quote: A quiet year does not create a cushion for us.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** includes checking each claim against the ledger.
Her husband's **market takings** vary while the mortgage date does not.
The **saved dinner cost** is a small feasible addition to a thin reserve.

steps.text: Keep answering billing calls and checking AI summaries against the ledger
Skip one bought family dinner each week
Save the skipped dinner cost for the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the easy billing replies may move to software, so our remaining calls need a fair time target. I would show my supervisor the errors I caught before anyone cuts the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my hours could shrink even with years on the floor. I'm good enough at ordinary calls, but not an expert in complex disputes, and few other centres sit nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll compare twenty old billing cases with the new answer tool on paid time and record wrong fees. If my hours fall in the first year, I'll apply for a posted paid care-assistant vacancy only if its wage and hours cover our mortgage; I will keep the centre wage until a written offer exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, close to alarmed. A missing shift would show up in the bank account before I learned another trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would check your tool test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask another agent to check my twenty cases and bring the error count to our team meeting. A fast wrong fee still sends a caller back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you know about care work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the care home what its assistants actually do during a full shift. Helping my mother after surgery taught me patience, but it was not paid care work.

say: I'd ask for a **fair call target** when easy replies vanish.
I'd show **caught fee errors** before the centre changes staffing.
think: I expect my **hours** could shrink despite experience.
I know **few nearby centres** and a thin reserve leave little search time.
do: Test **twenty old cases** with the answer tool on paid time.
Bring **checked error counts** with another agent to the team meeting.
Apply for **posted paid care work** after cuts only if wages and hours cover mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about a missing shift hitting the bank balance.
S1.quote: Helping my mother after surgery taught me patience, but it was not paid care work.
fieldNote: She uses **tool errors** as evidence before a staffing change.
Her **family experience** is not mistaken for professional care training.
She keeps the **current wage** until a written offer arrives.

steps.text: Test twenty old billing cases on paid time; present checked errors with another agent
Apply for posted paid care work after cuts only if wages and hours cover mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say general AI by 2028 could handle all the billing checks on my screen. Robots doing hands-on work around 2031 come later, but our call jobs do not get that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my post could end and the nearby centres might stop hiring too. My husband's market stall alone cannot pay the mortgage and two children's bills, and our savings are below one month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll copy our bills and ask for a written staffing date. If my role ends in the first year after 2028, I'll apply for advertised paid home-care work only if the wages and hours cover our bills; I'll ask my sister for school pickup only if she can spare the time on interview days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I have a list of calls to make, but almost no money for the gap between jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What purchase goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my husband we should postpone the new washing machine if the old one stays safe to use. A new payment plan is a poor answer to a lost wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can your sister cover school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister works shifts too, so her help isn't automatic. I would check her days before booking an interview or promising the children a lift.

say: I'd warn **2028 thinking AI** could take our billing calls.
I'd say **2031 robots** give headsets no extra years.
think: I expect my **post could end** with few nearby centres hiring.
I know my husband's **market income** cannot cover mortgage and children alone.
do: Copy bills and seek **written staffing dates**; postpone the washer only while the old one remains safe.
Apply for **advertised paid care work** after a real cut only if wages and hours cover bills.
Ask my **sister for pickup** only if her shifts leave time on interview days.
feel: **Alarmed** by an almost empty reserve and a job gap.
S2.quote: My husband's market stall alone cannot pay the mortgage and two children's bills, and our savings are below one month.
fieldNote: Her **market-income risk** compounds a possible cut to call work.
Her **sister's help** depends on real shift availability.
She postpones a **washing machine** only while the current one is safe.

steps.text: Apply for advertised paid care work after cuts only if wages and hours cover bills
Ask sister for school pickup only if her shifts allow interview-day help
Postpone washing machine purchase only while the old one remains safe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years gives us time to learn on paid shifts and check which new jobs are real. Our calls face general AI in 2031; hands-on robots come around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could become better at the hard billing cases before 2031, but that does not guarantee a job after AGI. A care home might offer paid work while hands-on tasks remain, and I need to see the actual hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep my billing shift and ask the care home about a supervised paid trial. If it posts a paid place with wages and hours covering our mortgage and funds the required care course, I'll complete the course on paid time; in the first year after 2031 I'll move only on a written offer that still meets those terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can check a full day. Five years lets me see the early start and the hard parts before relying on care wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the care trial show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to see lifting, cleaning and how the staff respond when someone is frightened. I don't want a pretty tour to stand in for a real shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who covers school pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband would have to cover school pickup while I trained. If his market day would be lost, the care wage must cover that loss too.

say: I'd seek **paid learning** during the five-year window while the centre still needs experienced agents.
I'd separate **2031 call risk** from later 2034 robots.
think: I could improve **hard billing** before 2031 if the centre still gives me paid calls.
I cannot count on **care wages** without checking real hours.
do: Keep my **paid billing shift** while available.
Complete **funded care course** on paid time only for a posted role whose wages and hours cover the mortgage.
Move after 2031 only on a **written paid offer** whose hours and wages cover mortgage and lost pickup income.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to inspect a full care shift.
S3.quote: I don't want a pretty tour to stand in for a real shift.
fieldNote: She asks about **lifting and cleaning**, not a polished visit.
Her **course path** requires paid time and a real posted role.
A **lost market day** must be covered by the new wage.

steps.text: Keep taking paid billing calls while shifts remain
Complete funded care course on paid time only for posted role with mortgage-covering wages and hours
Move only on written paid offer covering mortgage and lost market wages with sufficient hours
Try a supervised paid care shift if the care home offers one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my family a decade is enough to test new work without leaving a wage on a guess. Our calls face general AI in 2036; hands-on robots follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 the children may be older, but the mortgage could still be due. I could learn to review difficult claims or test care work, though neither is a guaranteed refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll keep my calls and transfer a small amount from each pay to the mortgage account. I'll check posted care openings twice a year; in the first year after 2036 I'll apply only if my centre hours fall and a written paid offer gives enough hours and wages for our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the future and anxious about today's short reserve. Ten years gives me room to act in small steps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the children to ask what a job pays before paying for training. Experience is good, but the mortgage is paid with wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a care trial early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the care home offered a paid trial, I'd check the journey and pickup plan before accepting it. My husband's market earnings change by day. We cannot lose both wages to test one role.

say: I'd test **new paid work** over the decade while our current call wages still cover bills.
I'd distinguish **2036 call work** from robots around 2039.
think: I may still have a **mortgage at 53**.
I cannot treat **claims or care work** as certain long-term shelter.
do: Keep my **call shift** while it pays.
Save a **small amount** from each payday for the mortgage.
Apply after 2036 only if **hours fall** and a written paid care offer covers household bills.
feel: **Uneasy** about future work and anxious about today's thin cushion.
S4.quote: We cannot lose both wages to test one role.
fieldNote: Her **thin reserve** keeps the decade scenario anxious today.
She checks **journey and pickup** before any paid trial.
She keeps **current pay** until a written care offer covers bills.

steps.text: Keep answering paid billing calls while shifts remain
Save small payday amounts toward the mortgage reserve
Apply after call cuts only for written paid care offer with hours and wages covering bills
Accept paid care trial only after checking journey, pickup and both household wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. It could end my billing calls while a mortgage and two children's bills continue, and our reserve is tiny. Written notice, a posted paid care role and funded training on paid time would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a machine's wrong fee before a family pays it. A neat summary can carry a mistake all the way to a real bill. Somebody must own the correction.

headlineQuote: A neat summary can carry a mistake all the way to a real bill.
portrait: Daria is an **experienced 43-year-old agent** with secondary schooling and average skill on billing calls.
Her **low pay**, savings below one month and few nearby centres sit beside a mortgage and two school-age children.
Her husband's **market takings** vary; she uses AI daily while verifying every amount against the ledger.
She tests **care work** only through paid, supervised options and needs a funded course and written bill-covering offer before moving.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her billing wage before a paid care place opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a posted paid care role would let her plan.
**Funded paid training** would keep course costs out of the mortgage account.
